reference.source: Postgraduate Haematology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: An X-linked recessive deficiency of coagulation factor VIII from mutations in F8, so it predominantly affects males while females are usually carriers
Bleeding is of the coagulation-factor type: recurrent haemarthroses, deep muscle haematomas and prolonged bleeding after trauma or surgery rather than mucocutaneous petechiae
Clinical severity is graded by residual factor VIII activity into severe, moderate and mild disease, and recurrent joint bleeds lead to chronic haemophilic arthropathy
The screening pattern is a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time and normal platelet count
A mixing study that corrects points to factor deficiency, and a specific factor VIII assay confirms the diagnosis and severity
A major complication of treatment is the development of neutralising alloantibodies (inhibitors) against factor VIII, which should be suspected when bleeding stops responding to replacement
Management uses factor VIII replacement or non-factor haemostatic therapies, desmopressin for some milder cases, and antifibrinolytics, with prophylaxis to prevent joint damage in severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Haemophilia A is caused by mutations in F8 on the X chromosome that reduce the activity of coagulation factor VIII, a cofactor that greatly accelerates factor IXa-mediated activation of factor X within the intrinsic tenase complex. Without adequate factor VIII the propagation phase of coagulation is impaired, so thrombin generation on the platelet surface is markedly reduced and the fibrin clot forms slowly and is unstable. Because the initial platelet plug still forms, bleeding is typically delayed and occurs into joints and deep tissues; repeated haemarthroses cause synovial inflammation and progressive destructive arthropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Von Willebrand disease (which lowers factor VIII secondarily)
Acquired haemophilia from factor VIII autoantibodies
Vitamin K deficiency or anticoagulant effect
additionalInvestigations: Activated partial thromboplastin time, prothrombin time and platelet count
Mixing study to distinguish factor deficiency from an inhibitor
Factor VIII activity assay to confirm diagnosis and grade severity
Von Willebrand factor studies to exclude von Willebrand disease
Factor VIII inhibitor (Bethesda) assay when response to replacement is poor
F8 genetic testing including the intron 22 inversion, for diagnosis and carrier detection
redFlags: Intracranial haemorrhage, which may follow minor or no recognised trauma
Airway-threatening neck, throat or retropharyngeal bleeding
Compartment syndrome from an expanding muscle haematoma
Loss of response to factor replacement suggesting an inhibitor
reference.prognosis: With prophylactic replacement or modern non-factor therapies most patients achieve near-normal life expectancy and greatly reduced joint damage, but inhibitor development and established arthropathy remain important sources of morbidity.
pitfalls: Missing von Willebrand disease as the reason for a low factor VIII level
Overlooking an inhibitor when bleeding fails to respond to appropriate replacement
Giving intramuscular injections or arterial punctures that provoke deep bleeding
Delaying treatment of a suspected head bleed to await imaging or laboratory confirmation
management: Prevent bleeds with prophylactic factor VIII replacement or the subcutaneous bispecific antibody emicizumab, and treat acute bleeds with factor VIII concentrate
Use desmopressin to raise endogenous factor VIII in mild disease, and add an antifibrinolytic such as tranexamic acid for mucosal or dental bleeding
Consider adeno-associated-virus gene therapy in eligible adults to achieve durable endogenous factor VIII expression
Manage inhibitors with immune tolerance induction and control bleeding with bypassing agents such as recombinant activated factor VII or activated prothrombin complex concentrate
Support joint health with physiotherapy and avoid intramuscular injections and NSAIDs that aggravate bleeding
Monitor factor levels, screen periodically for inhibitors, and assess joint status for early arthropathy
Manage through a specialist haemophilia treatment centre with multidisciplinary input
Offer genetic counselling and carrier testing to female relatives
